extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in classical Euclidean geometry / mathematicians interested in circle tangency problems and historical treatments (Apollonius, Pappus, Lagrange, Lhuilier)
extracted.subtask_description: Derive and classify the equations of lines tangent to two given circles (the common tangents), present existence/number-of-tangent cases, give algebraic and geometric constructions, and survey historical trigonometrical/constructive solutions of related Apollonian porism problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation of the common tangent (general algebraic form)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explicit algebraic equation (derived via substitution and completing the square) gives the common tangent(s) to two circles; the final expression (equation (23) in the text) depends on parameters p and R, each of which can take two values, so the expression yields four distinct equations corresponding to up to four common tangents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by eliminating variables between circle equations and the general line equation, substitute intermediate parametrisations (p, R, etc.), complete the square and extract; note that because p and R each have two signs/values, the algebraic formula splits into four possible lines. The text gives the explicit long-form expression (23) and notes that 'there are four lines which can each be drawn to touch the two given circles.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent existence & enumeration cases (classification 1–4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of the number (and reality) of common tangents depending on relationships among circle radii p1,p2 and centre distance d (and derived quantities R'): enumerated cases decide whether 0,1,2, or 4 tangents occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As stated: (1) If circles intersect: p1 + p2 > d and |p1 − p2| < d, then two tangents are real (two others imaginary). (2) If one circle lies wholly within the other: both p1 + p2 and p1 − p2 greater than d, R imaginary, so no common tangent. (3) If circles touch externally: p1 + p2 = d (and d > |p1 − p2|), two tangents correspond; when d^2 − (p1 + p2)^2 = 0 the two other tangents coalesce giving a single tangent at point of contact. (4) If one circle lies within and touches the other: d^2 − (p1 − p2)^2 = 0 (with the other R negative), yielding a single tangent. The text explains which radicals become imaginary/zero and how that affects the count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangency condition for a line to be tangent to a circle (quadratic discriminant = 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: For circle x^2 + y^2 = R^2 and line y = ax + b, substituting produces (1 + a^2)x^2 + 2ab x + (b^2 − R^2) = 0; tangency requires that this quadratic be a perfect square (discriminant zero), yielding the condition b^2 = (1 + a^2) R^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use substitution of the line into the circle equation, require double root (discriminant zero) so the resulting quadratic is a complete square. The same criterion is used analogously for both circles when deriving common tangent parameters; the text presents this as the algebraic condition that ensures a line is tangent to a circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportions locating abscissas where common tangents meet the centre-line
rubrics_metrics.description: If a is the abscissa where a common tangent meets the axis (the line of centres), then the relations R − r : R :: d : a and R + r : R :: d : a hold (two proportions are obtained corresponding to internal/external tangents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the trig/coordinate derivation eliminating parameters, one obtains the two proportions R−r : R :: d : a and R + r : R :: d : a, which give the (two) abscissas (C and C') on the line joining the centres where the two pairs of common tangents meet. The passage explains a geometric construction from these proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric construction of abscissas (construction recipe)
rubrics_metrics.description: A constructive geometric method: from centre A of the greater circle take radius AD, cut off DE = r and produce the radius to DF = r; join EB, FB to centre B, then draw from D lines parallel to EB and FB to meet AB in C and C'. These C, C' are the points where the common tangents meet the line joining the centres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedure reduces the common-tangent problem to the classical problem of drawing tangents from a given point to a given circle; the text outlines the exact steps and explains that each pair of tangents can be constructed from the corresponding C or C'. It ties back to the algebraic proportions for abscissas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersections of tangent pairs: loci and perpendicularity (poles of similitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: The intersection points of certain tangent-pairs lie on the line joining the centres; the line through the intersection of a pair of tangents is perpendicular to the line joining the centres. These intersections correspond to the external and internal poles of similitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic manipulation of the two tangent-equations (adding/subtracting the ±R versions) yields linear equations (24) and (25)/(26): subtraction gives the line through the centres, addition gives the line through the tangents' intersection perpendicular to the centres-line. The text remarks that these are, in modern terms, the external and internal poles of similitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for sign choices in parameters (internal vs external tangents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The different sign choices for parameters (e.g., X = ±, sign of p_i, and the two values of R from radicals d^2 − (p1 ± p2)^2) produce different species of tangents: those passing between the centres vs those not passing between the centres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text analyzes substitutions with ± and explains how changing signs leads to tangents whose intersection lies on the centres-line (when subtracting) or perpendicular (when adding), and which algebraic factors (p1 ± p2, R variants) determine the different geometric species (external/internal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pappus porism (enunciated porism / porismatic data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Porism: If from two given points A, B straight lines AC, BC are drawn to any point C in a given circle meeting it again in D, E respectively, and DE is drawn, then DE will (for each extremity) either contain a given angle with a line drawn from one extremity to a given point, or be parallel to a given line, or converge to a given point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text highlights that the essential poristic data (what is to be considered 'given') are printed in a distinct type in the original source; the porism is used as a structural device in solving Apollonius-type tangency problems and is particularly relevant for inscribing polygons with sides through given points. The author discusses prior analyses (Noble, Simson) and their relation to the porism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometrical approach for inscribing triangle with sides through three given points (Lagrange/Castillon method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up unknown central angles for triangle vertices and derive three tangent-based equations of the form tan(unknown) tan(known combination) = given; reduce these via substitutions (introducing p,q, etc.) to algebraic relations which ultimately reduce to a quadratic in one variable that is solvable and therefore constructible by ruler and compass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents Lagrange's/trigonometrical method: denote AO, BO, CO by a,b,c and unknown central angles by x,y,z; form three equations relating tangents of these angles, introduce substitutions tan(...) = p,q,r etc.; manipulate to obtain an equation of degree two in an auxiliary variable s (expressible with given data) so that solutions for angles (and hence vertex positions) follow. The historical account notes that although the algebraic final equation is complex, it reduces to a quadratic and hence is constructible; Lexell, Lhuilier and others produced constructions/expositions based on this reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lhuilier basis identities for trig-based solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary trig identities used as the foundational relations for Lagrange's solution: e.g., for an isosceles triangle ACA' with equal sides AC = CA' and lines CB, CB' to base (or its extension), CA + CB : CA − CB :: 1 : tan(ACB) tan(A'CB), and similar identities for CB' and CA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lhuilier states these as simple propositions forming the 'basis' for the trigonometrical solutions; the text remarks these identities underlie Lagrange's process and the trigonometrical reductions carried out by subsequent authors for polygonal/tangency problems. The author summarizes Lhuilier's more general propositions concerning sums/differences and products of tangents and their solvability for small numbers of arcs.
